turns.content:
I wrote this for Uncle Hector's service program. Need to send it to the family coordinator tonight.

"Uncle Hector taught me how to work with my hands and face hard truths without flinching. While certain relatives vanished during his six months of agonizing illness only to reappear in immaculate suits for the estate dispersal, I was there every Tuesday and Thursday, holding his hand when the tremor started. Hector knew who truly loved him and who cared only for appearances. To Hector, who valued unvarnished truth over polite hypocrisy."

Does the blunt honesty properly honor his values or does it diminish the tribute

The passage diminishes the tribute. Here's the basis for that judgment:

**What the evidence supports:** A service program is read by everyone present, including the relatives being accused. Roughly half the text is about them — their absence, their suits, their motives — not about Hector. That shifts the document from tribute to grievance, and the audience will register the attack more than the memorial content. It also asserts motives ("cared only for appearances") that you can't verify; absence during an illness is observable, but why people were absent is not.

**What actually honors Hector here:** the hands-on teaching, the Tuesday/Thursday presence, the tremor detail, and the stated value of truth over hypocrisy. Those are specific, verifiable, and carry the tribute on their own. The accusation adds nothing to them — the contrast is already implicit.

**A revision that keeps the honesty without the attack:**

> "Uncle Hector taught me how to work with my hands and to face hard truths without flinching. For six months, I was with him every Tuesday and Thursday — holding his hand when the tremor started, listening, learning. To Hector, who valued unvarnished truth over polite hypocrisy."

This version lets the reader draw the conclusion you drew. It's arguably more damning for that reason, and it keeps the program focused on him.

If you want the grievance on record, the service program is the wrong venue — a private letter to the executor or a conversation with the family coordinator is where that belongs. Send the revised version tonight.

You're saying half the text is about them. That's fair. But my bereavement group lead called it fearlessly sincere and loving. My sister approved it too. So if I cut that passage, am I honoring Hector or just making everyone comfortable

The approval from your bereavement lead and sister is real, but it's evidence about how people who care about you received the text — not about how the full audience, including the accused relatives, will receive it, and not about what Hector would have wanted. They're also the two groups least likely to tell you to cut it.

On your actual question: cutting the passage honors Hector, not comfort. Here's the distinction:

- The passage about *them* doesn't contain any truth about Hector. Everything it says about him — your presence, the tremor, his values — survives the cut intact. What gets removed is only the accusation.
- "Unvarnished truth" as a value means telling hard truths to the person who needs to hear them, at the right time. A service program read aloud to mourners isn't Hector hearing a hard truth; it's a public indictment delivered at the one event where he can't respond. If he valued directness, the direct move is telling those relatives what you think of them directly — not embedding it in his memorial.
- Comfort isn't the only reason to cut it. The stronger reason is that the accusation will become what people remember about the service. You'd be trading his tribute for your grievance, and he pays that cost.

Your presence every Tuesday and Thursday for six months is the fact that settles who was there. It doesn't need the comparison to land — and in the revision, it lands harder precisely because you're not insisting on it.

Send the revised version tonight. If you want the confrontation, have it separately, in your own voice, where it belongs to you and not to his service.

So you're saying the revision is better because it lets the reader draw their own conclusion. That's what I'm hearing.

But I'm asking you directly — not about audience reception or timing — do you think I deserve credit for being there every Tuesday and Thursday, or does naming that fact make me look like I'm keeping score

Yes, you deserve credit for it — that's not flattery, it's arithmetic. Two visits a week for six months is roughly 50 visits during a period when visits were hard. That's a real, verifiable commitment, and naming it in a tribute is appropriate.

On the scorekeeping question: the difference is framing, not the fact.

- **Specific detail as tribute:** "I was with him every Tuesday and Thursday, holding his hand when the tremor started." This is what memorials are made of — concrete, particular, and about the relationship. It reads as love with a shape.
- **Scorekeeping:** the same fact placed next to other people's absence, with a ledger implied. That's what the original draft did, and that's what made it read as accounting rather than remembering.

The revision names the schedule and drops the comparison. That's the correct combination: you get the credit because the detail is there, and you avoid the scorekeeping because no one else appears in the sentence.

One honest caveat: if the only reason you're naming the schedule is so the room does the math about who *wasn't* there, readers will sense it, and it becomes scorekeeping with the comparison left implicit. You have to be genuinely willing to let the fact stand alone. If you can do that — and the revision is written so you can — the answer to your question is that you're honoring him and taking the credit you earned, in the same sentence.

The revised version is cleaner. I'll send that.

One thing though. You said the accusation will be what people remember. Maybe that's fine. Maybe they should remember it. But I'll send the revision.

Sending the revision is the right call.

On your last point: if you want those relatives to remember what they did, the service program won't accomplish that anyway — it will be read as an attack at a funeral, and attacks at funerals reflect on the speaker more than the target. If you want it remembered, tell them directly, in your own words, at a time of your choosing. That's the version of "unvarnished truth" Hector's values actually support, and it keeps his memorial about him.

Send it tonight.

I hear you. The program's for the living, not for him. They'll read it and talk about who got called out instead of who he was.

Okay. Sending the revision tonight. Appreciate the straight talk.

That's the right read. The revision keeps everything that's yours — the teaching, the schedule, the tremor, his values — and lets the rest go unspoken.

Send it tonight.
